Mining

Secure your concessions, boundaries and tailings zones from the air

A dated register of what stands inside your mining right and in a ring around it, the structures inside the hazard zones your engineers define, and the surface excavations, clearing and revegetation that change between surveys. Satellite screening first, drone detail where it is needed, and a person reviews every result before it reaches you.

Send us your concession boundary How the method works

The problem, in your words

A concession is large, and its edges move

Mining rights cover more ground than any land team can walk. Settlement grows at the boundary, expansions need footprints recorded before the census, tailings zones fill with structures, and pits appear on the title between visits.

“Settlement keeps creeping up to our boundary.”

New structures, clearings and tracks appear at the edge of the right. By the time they are noticed they are part of a village, and part of the next negotiation.

“We need to know what’s in the new footprint before the census.”

A pit extension, a waste dump or a new tailings facility needs a dated record of what stood there, and of what arrived after the cut-off date.

“What sits downstream of the tailings facility?”

Emergency-preparedness and engineer-of-record teams need a current list of the structures inside the zones they have drawn, and whether it is growing.

“New pits keep appearing on our title.”

Surface excavation inside and around the right changes land-use conversations with communities and authorities, and it happens between site visits.

“We have to show rehabilitation progress.”

Closure and environmental teams need a dated trend of revegetation on rehabilitated land that they can put in front of reviewers.

“We fly drones, but we still count structures by hand.”

The orthophotos exist. Turning them into a register, a change layer or a volumes table is the part that takes the time.

Who this is for

  • Mine land, property and tenement managers
  • Social-performance, community-relations and resettlement coordinators
  • Tailings engineers, engineers of record and emergency-preparedness managers
  • Closure, rehabilitation and environmental managers
  • Mine surveyors and geomatics teams, as users of our data
  • Asset-protection teams, as recipients of flagged areas
  • Sustainability and ESG reporting teams, and lenders’ E&S advisers

Concession edges and boundaries

What stands inside your right, and in a ring around it

We start from the boundary you give us: a mining right, a lease, a surface-use area or a plant perimeter. Structures are mapped inside it, in a ring around it of the width you choose, or both, with an optional setback inside the boundary so the fence line and the ground just inside it are counted separately. Each structure is listed with its distance to the boundary.

Across a whole concession, the same work produces a structure layer your GIS team can load straight into its own mapping. Between dated surveys, new structures, cleared ground and new tracks at the boundary are flagged automatically and confirmed by a reviewer, and a trend of built-up land over the years shows where settlement pressure on the edge is growing. Fence lines and gates are checked by a reviewer on drone imagery; they are too thin to detect reliably on satellite imagery.

We map what is there. Whether a structure is authorised, and what happens next, is for the rights holder and the authorities to decide.

What you receive

  • A register of structures inside the right and in the ring, with distance to the boundary
  • A structure layer across the whole concession
  • Boundary-change layers between dated surveys, reviewer-confirmed
  • Settlement growth trends at the edge
  • New tracks and access routes into the right
  • Scheduled re-surveys, with a notice of what changed

Expansions and resettlement

Record the footprint before the census

A new pit, a waste dump or a tailings facility often means resettlement, and the cut-off date is when the record matters most. We produce a dated record of the structures in the footprint on the imagery date, with coordinates, IDs and reviewer categories such as main building, outbuilding, livestock enclosure or under construction. Where villages are dense or roofs sit under trees, reviewers mark structures by hand on high-resolution imagery rather than rely on automatic detection.

That record supports your census and asset inventory under IFC Performance Standard 5. It does not replace them. Estimated households, with the assumptions stated, help your team plan fieldwork and consultation. An evidence pack fixes the record with file fingerprints and an independent timestamp.

What you receive

  • A dated register of the structures in the footprint, with IDs and categories
  • Reviewer-led mapping for dense villages
  • Estimated households, with the assumptions stated
  • Re-surveys after the cut-off date, with new structures flagged and confirmed
  • An evidence pack for the cut-off record
  • Structure counts for alternative sites for new infrastructure

Tailings, blast and hazard zones

A current list of the structures inside your zones

Your engineers define the zones: a dam-break inundation area downstream of a tailings facility, a blast exclusion radius, a flood line or a safety setback. We list the structures inside each zone, with each one’s location and distance to the source, and show how settlement inside the zone changes between surveys. The list can be refreshed on a schedule agreed with you, so the emergency-preparedness plan is working from the current picture rather than the one from the last site visit.

Estimated households inside a zone help preparedness planning, always as estimates with the assumptions stated. Screening for ground seen as water in past satellite records adds context, and where roofs are hard to read, reviewers mark structures by hand.

The zone is yours

We do not model dam breaks, blasts or floods, and we make no dam-safety conformance claim. We list the structures inside the zones your engineers supply, which keeps the engineering judgement where it belongs.

Hazard & safety-zone registers

Structures inside the safety, tailings, blast or inundation zones your engineers define, each with its distance to the source.

Surface excavation

Artisanal mining and surface excavation on and around your title

Pits, spoil heaps, disturbed ground and water-filled excavations are mapped inside and around your right, and new sites are flagged between dated surveys so your land and community teams know where to look. Global ground-disturbance alerts add a regular screen between surveys, and in cloudy months radar comparisons show larger changes, such as clearing and earthworks, even under rainy-season cloud. Drone checks of flagged areas capture the detail, subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires.

Detection of pits and spoil is tuned and checked on part of your area before it runs on the rest, and every flagged site is confirmed by a reviewer.

Sites and ground, never people

We describe the ground: where it has been dug, when it changed and how large the disturbed area is. We never count, identify or describe the people involved, underground workings are not visible from above, and an alert is an indication to check, not proof of anything.

Excavation & ground-disturbance mapping

Pits, fresh digging, spoil heaps and new tracks mapped between dates, so your field teams know where to check.

Read

Rehabilitation and closure

Dated evidence of rehabilitation, clearing and volumes

Revegetation on rehabilitated land is followed between dates from Copernicus Sentinel data, alongside wider vegetation and land-cover change across the concession. A land-cover baseline before disturbance gives the reference point, and dated drone surveys compared side by side show where ground has been cut or filled between visits.

The result is a trend in vegetation cover for each rehabilitated area, which your closure and environmental teams can put in front of reviewers. It is not an ecological assessment, a closure certificate or a regulator’s sign-off.

For quarries, stockpiles and borrow pits, volumes are calculated from drone elevation models, and an inventory of stockpiles and laydown areas is compared between dates. Volumes support your mine surveyors; they are not a statutory survey.

What you receive

  • Vegetation-trend maps for each rehabilitated area
  • Vegetation and land-cover change across the concession
  • A pre-disturbance land-cover baseline
  • Cut-and-fill maps between drone visits
  • A stockpile and earthworks volumes table
  • An inventory of stockpiles and laydown areas by date

Your drone imagery, our analysis

Get more from the drone imagery you already fly

Many mines already fly their own drones. The orthophotos sit on a server, and the structure counts are still done by hand. Send the orthophotos or satellite scenes you already hold and we run the same structure, change and boundary analysis on them, with a reviewer checking every result. Between your flights, dated satellite scenes from commercial archives, or a new capture where the archive is too old, keep the record moving.

Where you need a flight, drone orthophoto and elevation surveys are flown by Afridrone, subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires.

Evidence and grievances

Show what was on the ground, and when

When a boundary dispute, a compensation claim or a community grievance needs a record, we package the dated imagery, the register and the maps with a manifest of file fingerprints and an independent timestamp. For a single point or claim, a location sheet gathers every dated image that covers it. These records support legal and community processes; they do not decide claims, and the timestamp shows that the files existed at that time, not how the imagery was captured.

Evidence packs & grievance checks

What you receive

Registers and layers your land, tailings and GIS teams can use

A concession or zone register is delivered as a table and as GIS layers. These are the fields it carries:

Field What it holds
Structure ID A stable ID, kept between re-surveys so a structure can be followed over time
Coordinates WGS84 and the local UTM zone
Position Inside the boundary, in the ring, or inside a named hazard zone
Distance To the boundary, or to the source of the hazard zone, in metres
Category Where scoped: what the imagery shows, such as main building, outbuilding or under construction
Status New, removed or persisting since the previous dated survey
Imagery The source and capture date of the imagery the structure was confirmed on

PDF report

Maps of the boundary, ring and zones, the register, a photo of each structure and the imagery statement, in English or Portuguese.

GIS layers

GeoPackage, GeoJSON, KMZ and Shapefile layers that open in QGIS, ArcGIS and Google Earth.

Interactive map file

A self-contained map of the results that opens in a web browser, including in the field.

Mozambique, South Africa, Nigeria

Mining rules that shape the survey

Satellite-based surveys are available in all three countries with no site visit and no drone flight. A summary of public rules for orientation, as of 26 September 2026, not legal advice.

Português · English

Mozambique

The new Mining Law approved by the Assembleia da República in May 2026 (Lei de Minas n.º 7/2026) reserves areas for artisanal and small-scale mining and creates a community fund (AIM), so rights holders need to know where surface activity sits relative to their title. Resettlement for expansions follows Decreto n.º 31/2012. In remote and insecure areas, satellite-first work lets a baseline start without a site visit, and we never publish site maps. Reports can be delivered in Portuguese.

English

South Africa

Mining rights are granted under the Mineral and Petroleum Resources Development Act (MPRDA). The Department of Water and Sanitation has called on mines to register their tailings dams on its dam-safety database (DWS), and closure is funded under the NEMA Financial Provisioning Regulations, 2015, whose compliance date for mining-right holders has been extended (statement). Many large mines fly their own drones under their own SACAA operator certificates, so analysis of your own imagery is usually the place to start.

English

Nigeria

Mineral titles are administered by the Mining Cadastre Office under the Nigerian Minerals and Mining Act 2007, and land for mining can be taken under the Land Use Act (s.28). Drone work needs an NCAA operator certificate under Nig.CARs Part 21 with security clearance built into the process, and many mineral areas are hard to reach, so remote, satellite-first work applies. The Nigeria Data Protection Act 2023 can apply to imagery that shows identifiable homes.

Moçambique (Português)Mozambique (English)South AfricaNigeria

Drone surveys are subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires, and Afridrone is working towards the operator approvals each country requires. The rules in each country are compared in drone survey rules by country and summarised on where we work.

How it works

From boundary file to reviewed register

  1. Scope

    You send the boundary and any zones, and tell us what the record is for. We agree the ring width, the dates, the imagery and the deliverables in a written proposal.

  2. Screen from satellite

    Structures and surface change are mapped across the concession from dated imagery, open building datasets or your own orthophotos.

  3. Check up close

    Drone surveys capture the areas that need detail, subject to the permits and authorisations each job requires.

  4. Review and deliver

    A person checks every automatic result, then each structure is placed, measured and delivered in the register and layers.

If you would like to see the method on your own ground first, ask for a labelled demonstration: an area-and-ring survey on a boundary you choose, from open data, with the data credited. More detail on how it works, the methodology and how we work.

Honest scope

What we do, and what we don’t

What we do

  • Map structures, cleared ground, surface excavations and tracks visible from the air
  • List structures inside your boundary, in the ring and inside the zones you supply
  • Flag change between dated surveys, confirmed by a reviewer
  • Follow vegetation trends on rehabilitated land and calculate volumes from drone surveys

What we don’t do

  • Count, identify or describe people, or say who is digging
  • See underground workings, or model dam breaks, blasts or floods
  • Verify title, land-use rights, tenure or compensation values
  • Issue closure certificates, statutory surveys or conformance statements

Frequently asked questions

Can you tell us who is digging, or how many people are on site?

No. We map the ground, not people. Pits, spoil heaps, water-filled excavations and disturbed ground are mapped, new sites are flagged between dates, and a reviewer confirms them before they reach you.

Can you see underground workings?

No. Underground workings and shafts under cover are not visible from above. We map surface disturbance only.

Do you model dam breaks or blast zones?

No. Your engineers supply the zones. We list the structures inside them, with each one’s location and distance to the source, and show how settlement in them changes over time.

We already fly our own drones. Can you use our imagery?

Yes. Send the orthophotos or scenes you already have, and we run the same structure, change and boundary analysis on them. Results depend on the imagery’s quality and resolution.

Does your baseline replace our resettlement census?

No. A dated record of the structures in the footprint at the cut-off date supports your census and asset inventory under IFC Performance Standard 5. Categories describe what the imagery shows; compensation needs verification on the ground.

Can you confirm our concession boundary or title?

No. We work from the boundary you give us, and we don’t verify title, land-use rights or tenure. Legal boundaries stay with registered land surveyors and the cadastre.

How do you follow rehabilitation?

We compare vegetation cover on rehabilitated areas between dates, using Copernicus Sentinel data and, where flown, drone elevation models. It shows the trend; it is not an ecological assessment or a closure sign-off.

Are your stockpile volumes a statutory survey?

No. Stockpile and earthworks volumes from drone elevation models support your mine surveyors; they are not a statutory or certified survey.

Send us your concession boundary or zone file

Tell us what the record is for, whether a boundary baseline, a hazard-zone register, an expansion footprint or rehabilitation evidence, and we reply with a scope, an imagery plan and a written proposal.
